newsitem.title: SPAIN: Disney denies plans for new Euro theme park.
newsitem.headline: Disney denies plans for new Euro theme park.

text.p: Entertainment giant Walt Disney Co. said Friday it had no plans to build a new theme park in Europe in addition to Disneyland Paris.

The company was reacting to comments by an official of the local government of Valencia, Spain, who said Disney was among several groups negotiating to build a theme park on the eastern coast of Spain.
The company said in a statement from Paris that it "had no other development project in Europe besides the site of Disneyland Paris."
The regional government was also in talks with Paramount and Universal Studios over plans to build a large theme park near the sun and sea resort of Alicante, she said.

"The regional president Eduardo Zaplana went to the U.S. with a delegation last week and met company heads, including at Disney, to discuss the construction of a theme park in the south of the region," the spokeswoman told Reuters.
The exact location of the theme park had not been decided but it will be in the province of Alicante, near the popular Costa Blanca tourist resort of the same name.

"We still don't know what type of park it would be and negotiations now centre on whether it would be better to build it together with one of the large groups or give it its own name, like Port Aventura," the official said.

The Spanish delegation met Disney officials in Orlando, Fla., last Thursday including the multinational's Spanish partner. They also met former Disney vice-chairman Steven Backer, now a theme park consultant.
Zaplana visited Disney and Universal theme parks in Orlando before heading to New York on Friday for talks with officials at Universal and Merrill Lynch.
Disney rejected Spain as a location for its first European project, picking Paris instead.

The Euro Disney leisure complex has had a rocky start and the outlook is still shaky although it is expected to make a profit in 1996 for the second year in a row. Rainy weather and a strong French franc have helped dampen sales.

If Valencia goes ahead with the construction of its own theme park, it would enter into direct competition with nearby Port Aventura, a $500 million theme park south of Barcelona which opened last year.
Port Aventura, majority-owned by British media group Pearson, has beaten forecasts by attracting thousands of visitors lured by warm southern temperatures and nearby beaches.
